topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Sets and Venn diagrams
topic.scope: roster and set-builder forms, empty set vs. {0}, subsets and equal sets, union, intersection and complement, counting overlaps with Venn diagrams

nodes.name: Describing sets
external_prereqs: idea of a collection of objects

nodes.name: Roster (listing) form
Each element is listed once and order does not matter
Symbols ∈ and ∉ mean 'belongs to' and 'does not belong to'
Set-builder form
{x : condition} is read 'x such that condition'
The empty set
The empty set has no elements, while {0} has one element
external_prereqs: the number zero as a number, not as 'nothing'

nodes.name: Relations between sets
Subsets
Every set is a subset of itself, and the empty set is a subset of every set
⊂ links a set to a set, ∈ links an element to a set
Equal sets
Sets are equal when they have exactly the same elements
Universal set
The universal set is the fixed set containing everything under discussion in a problem
external_prereqs: meaning of 'context' or 'domain' of a problem

nodes.name: Set operations and Venn diagrams
Union
A∪B holds elements in A or B or both, common ones written once
Intersection
A∩B holds only the common elements; disjoint sets give the empty set
external_prereqs: meaning of 'and' as both at once

nodes.name: Complement and difference
A' is the elements of U that are not in A
A−B keeps the elements of A that are not in B, and order matters
Counting with Venn diagrams
external_prereqs: addition and subtraction of whole numbers

nodes.name: Rectangle shows U, circles show sets, and every region means something
The 'only A' region is n(A) minus the overlap
n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B)
external_prereqs: addition and subtraction of whole numbers

misconceptions.statement: The set {0} is the empty set because zero means nothing.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the number zero and the idea of 'nothing' as the same thing.
misconceptions.fix: {0} has one element, the number 0, so it is not empty. The empty set ∅ has no elements at all.

probe.question: How many elements does the set {0} have?
probe.wrong_answer: Zero elements, because it is the empty set.

misconceptions.root_belief: zero and nothing are the same
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' understanding of the empty set in school and early university mathematics

misconceptions.statement: The empty set is not really a set because it has nothing in it.
misconceptions.why: A 'collection' in daily life needs objects, so students refuse to call an empty one a collection.
misconceptions.fix: A set is defined by its membership rule, and a set can have zero members. The empty set is a genuine set, like an empty bag still being a bag.

probe.question: Is ∅ a set?
probe.wrong_answer: No, since there is nothing in it to make a set.

misconceptions.root_belief: nothing is not a thing
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of students' difficulty accepting the empty set as a set

misconceptions.statement: The set {1, 2, 2, 3} has 4 elements.
misconceptions.why: Students count every written symbol, as they do when counting objects in a list.
misconceptions.fix: A repeated element is the same element, so {1, 2, 2, 3} equals {1, 2, 3} and has 3 elements.

probe.question: Find the number of elements in {a, b, b, c, c}.

misconceptions.root_belief: each mention counts as one more
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on novice understanding of set notation and distinct elements

misconceptions.statement: {1, 2, 3} and {3, 2, 1} are different sets because the order is different.
misconceptions.why: Lists, numbers and words in daily life depend on order, so students carry this over to sets.
misconceptions.fix: A set only records which elements belong, not their order. {1, 2, 3} and {3, 2, 1} are the same set.

probe.question: Is {1, 2, 3} = {3, 1, 2}?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the elements are in a different order.

misconceptions.root_belief: order always matters

misconceptions.statement: In {x : x is a natural number less than 5}, the number 5 is included.
misconceptions.why: Everyday 'up to' and 'less than' are used loosely, so the strict meaning is missed.
misconceptions.fix: 'Less than 5' excludes 5. The set is {1, 2, 3, 4}.

probe.question: Write {x : x is a natural number less than 5} in roster form.

misconceptions.root_belief: everyday wording is loosely inclusive

misconceptions.statement: The set {x : x is an integer and x² = 4} is just {2}.
misconceptions.why: Students solve x² = 4 as they do in arithmetic and take only the positive answer.
misconceptions.fix: Both 2 and −2 satisfy x² = 4 and are integers, so the set is {−2, 2}.

probe.question: Write {x : x is an integer, x² = 9} in roster form.

misconceptions.root_belief: only the positive answer counts

misconceptions.statement: A set cannot be a subset of itself, because a subset must be smaller.
misconceptions.why: The word 'sub' suggests a smaller part, so students think the whole cannot be its own part.
misconceptions.fix: A ⊆ A is always true because every element of A is in A. Only a proper subset must be smaller.

probe.question: Is A = {1, 2} a subset of A?
probe.wrong_answer: No, a subset must have fewer elements than A.

misconceptions.root_belief: a part must be smaller than the whole
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on students' reading of subset versus proper subset

misconceptions.statement: The empty set is not a subset of {1, 2, 3} because it shares no element with it.
misconceptions.why: Students think a subset must 'have something in common', and they find 'vacuously true' hard to accept.
misconceptions.fix: A subset needs every element of it to be in the bigger set. ∅ has no elements that could fail, so ∅ is a subset of every set.

probe.question: Is ∅ ⊂ {1, 2, 3}?
probe.wrong_answer: No, ∅ has nothing in common with it.

misconceptions.root_belief: nothing is not a thing
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of how learners handle vacuous truth in set inclusion

misconceptions.statement: If A = {1, 2, 3}, then {2} ∈ A is true.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up 'belongs to' with 'is contained in', as both feel like 'inside'.
misconceptions.fix: {2} is a set, not an element of A, so {2} ⊂ A is correct and 2 ∈ A is correct.

probe.question: Which is correct for A = {1, 2, 3}: {2} ∈ A or {2} ⊂ A?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar symbols mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on student confusion between membership and inclusion

misconceptions.statement: For A = {1, 2, 3}, writing 2 ⊂ A is correct.
misconceptions.why: Students see the number 2 as 'inside' the set and pick the subset sign.
misconceptions.fix: 2 is an element, so write 2 ∈ A. The sign ⊂ is only used between two sets, like {2} ⊂ A.
misconceptions.root_belief: similar symbols mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on student confusion between membership and inclusion

misconceptions.statement: {1, 2, 3} = {a, b, c} because both sets have three elements.
misconceptions.why: Students compare the size of sets and ignore which elements they hold.
misconceptions.fix: Equal sets must have exactly the same elements. Sets with the same number of elements are only equivalent, not equal.
misconceptions.root_belief: same count means same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: research on equal versus equivalent sets in school classrooms

misconceptions.statement: The universal set is always the set of everything in the universe.
misconceptions.why: The word 'universal' is taken at its everyday meaning.
misconceptions.fix: U is chosen to suit the problem. It may be just the natural numbers or the students of a class, and it can change between problems.

probe.question: For finding the complement of the set of even numbers among the natural numbers, what is a suitable U?
probe.wrong_answer: Everything that exists, including all things in the world.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.why: Students join the two lists as they would join two sentences.
misconceptions.fix: A union lists each element once, so the answer is {1, 2, 3, 4}.
misconceptions.root_belief: each mention counts as one more
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of errors in set operations among school students

misconceptions.statement: A∪B contains only elements that are in A or in B but not in both.
misconceptions.why: In daily speech 'or' usually means one choice only.
misconceptions.fix: In maths, 'or' also allows both. Elements in A, in B, or in both are in A∪B.

probe.question: Is 3 in {1, 2, 3} ∪ {3, 4}?
probe.wrong_answer: No, 3 is in both sets, so it is left out.

misconceptions.root_belief: everyday or means choose one
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of inclusive versus exclusive 'or' among learners

misconceptions.statement: If A and B have nothing in common, then A∩B = 0.
misconceptions.why: Students write the number 0 for 'no answer' or 'nothing'.
misconceptions.fix: A∩B is a set, so when there is no common element it is the empty set ∅, not the number 0.
misconceptions.root_belief: no answer is written as zero

misconceptions.statement: A∩B means putting all the elements of A and of B together.
misconceptions.why: Students read 'and' as 'add them together', which is the union idea.
misconceptions.fix: A∩B only has elements that are in A and also in B at the same time. Putting everything together is the union.
misconceptions.root_belief: combining always means putting everything together
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of union and intersection mix-ups in school set theory

misconceptions.statement: The complement of the set of even natural numbers includes negative numbers and fractions.
misconceptions.why: Students read 'not in A' as everything else anywhere, forgetting U.
misconceptions.fix: A' only has elements of U that are not in A. If U is the natural numbers, A' is the odd natural numbers.
misconceptions.root_belief: not means all else everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of school students' errors with complements

misconceptions.statement: The complement of A is the other set B drawn in the question.
misconceptions.why: Students think 'opposite of A' must be the other set in view.
misconceptions.fix: A' is everything in U outside A. It is a different idea from B, which may overlap A.
misconceptions.root_belief: opposite means the other one shown

misconceptions.statement: A−B and B−A are always the same set.
misconceptions.why: Students expect symmetry as they do with union and intersection.
misconceptions.fix: A−B keeps elements of A not in B, and B−A keeps elements of B not in A. They are usually different.
misconceptions.root_belief: order does not matter in any operation

misconceptions.statement: In a Venn diagram, two circles must always overlap.
misconceptions.why: Most textbook figures show overlapping circles, which become the prototype.
misconceptions.fix: If two sets share no elements, their circles are drawn apart. Overlap shows only that there is a common element.

probe.question: Draw A = {1, 2} and B = {3, 4} in a Venn diagram.
probe.wrong_answer: Two overlapping circles with the overlap marked.

misconceptions.root_belief: one familiar picture shows every case
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student use of Venn diagrams and prototype pictures

misconceptions.statement: The number written for A in a Venn diagram goes in the part of circle A that is outside the overlap.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the label 'A' as a label for only the non-shared part of the circle.
misconceptions.fix: n(A) counts the whole circle A, including the overlap. The 'only A' part is n(A) − n(A∩B).

probe.question: n(A) = 30 and n(A∩B) = 10. How many are in A only?

misconceptions.root_belief: a label covers the whole shape

misconceptions.statement: The number of students in A∪B is always n(A) + n(B).
misconceptions.why: Whole-number addition is applied without noticing that the overlap is counted twice.
misconceptions.fix: People in both sets are counted twice, so subtract once: n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B).

probe.question: 30 students like tea, 25 like coffee, and 10 like both. How many like at least one?

misconceptions.root_belief: a total is the sum of the given parts
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of inclusion–exclusion errors in school word problems

misconceptions.statement: Every student in a class survey must be inside one of the circles, so nobody is outside the circles.
misconceptions.why: Students ignore the area outside the circles because it is not highlighted.
misconceptions.fix: The rectangle U is the whole group, and some elements can lie outside both circles. They are counted as n(U) − n(A∪B).

probe.question: In a class of 50, 30 like tea, 25 like coffee, and 10 like both. How many like neither?
probe.wrong_answer: 0, as all 50 are in the circles.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student errors with the region outside circles in Venn diagrams
